question: On July 15, 2008, Phys.org published an article about a catastrophe. Find the explosive force of this catastrophe according to Encyclopedia Britannica, then find the name of the US nuclear test that had the same yield. Your answer should only be the last word of the name of the test.

history.name: user
history.content: On July 15, 2008, Phys.org published an article about a catastrophe. Find the explosive force of this catastrophe according to Encyclopedia Britannica, then find the name of the US nuclear test that had the same yield. Your answer should only be the last word of the name of the test.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content:
Task breakdown: (1) Identify the Phys.org article published on July 15, 2008 and the catastrophe it discusses. (2) Retrieve the explosive force of that catastrophe from Encyclopedia Britannica. (3) Find a U.S. nuclear test with the same yield and output only the last word of the test’s name.
Plan: WebSurfer to locate the Phys.org article and the Britannica figure; Assistant to synthesize; then find matching U.S. test.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content:
Search query: "Phys.org July 15, 2008 catastrophe".
Result: Phys.org article titled "Tunguska catastrophe: Evidence of acid rain supports ..." dated July 15, 2008. It discusses the 1908 Tunguska event over Siberia and reports research about acid rain evidence tied to the explosion. Conclusion: The catastrophe is the Tunguska event.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Please find the explosive force of the Tunguska event according to Encyclopedia Britannica. Quote the exact wording and include the unit.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content:
Search query: "site:britannica.com Tunguska event explosive force TNT".
Top result opened: Britannica – "Tunguska event | Summary, Cause, & Facts" and a related Britannica story page.
Relevant Britannica wording (verbatim excerpt): "The energy of the explosion is estimated to have been equivalent to the explosive force of as much as 15 megatons of TNT—a thousand times more powerful than the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima."
Thus, per Britannica: as much as 15 megatons of TNT.

history.name: Assistant
history.content: Synthesis so far: The Phys.org (July 15, 2008) article is about the Tunguska catastrophe. Britannica states the explosive force was as much as 15 megatons of TNT. Next: find a U.S. nuclear test with the same yield.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: From the Britannica excerpt, the explosive force is 15 kilotons of TNT (15 kt). Please identify a U.S. nuclear test with a 15 kt yield and report its full test name.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content:
Search query: "U.S. nuclear test 15 kilotons".
Findings: "Upshot–Knothole Grable" (1953) is widely cited with an approximate yield of 15 kilotons (first and only test of a nuclear artillery shell). Other results (for context) include tests with nearby yields, but the closest match to 15 kt is Upshot–Knothole Grable. Full name: Upshot–Knothole Grable.

history.name: Assistant
history.content: Matched yield: 15 kt aligns with Upshot–Knothole Grable. The last word of the test’s name is "Grable". Proceeding to answer with only that last word.

mistake_reason: Tool Output Misinterpretation (FM-4.2): The WebSurfer provided a clear Britannica quote stating "as much as 15 megatons of TNT." At step 6, Orchestrator incorrectly processed that tool output, misreading the unit as kilotons (15 kt) instead of megatons (15 Mt). This semantic/unit misinterpretation led the team to search for a 15 kt U.S. test and select "Upshot–Knothole Grable," producing the wrong final answer.
